title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether interposing a deterministic network verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated device configurations that would execute with operational faults in an isolated emulation environment. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics we evaluated 72 preregistered intent pairs with gpt-5-mini and a canonical verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 72 baseline executions produced no emulator‑observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected‑fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Under the executed contract the verifier therefore did not reduce undetected faults because none occurred in the baseline (a ceiling effect). We report preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, exact inferential outputs, and artifact‑grounded limitations that motivate alternative designs (adversarial tasks, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model sampling) required to evaluate verifier utility under realistic error regimes.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate high‑level operator intent into low‑level device configuration commands and thus offer potential productivity gains in network operations (NetOps). Prior controlled studies have demonstrated promising intent→configuration accuracy under constrained vendor dialects, while surveys and prototype systems emphasize operational risks such as semantic errors, incorrect command ordering, and protocol misuse that may cause outages or policy violations [1], [2]. A canonical mitigation pattern is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that places deterministic validators (e.g., header‑space or policy checkers) between generation and execution to detect violations before changes are applied [3], [4]. However, prior evidence quantifying how much a verifier reduces executed, undetected faults on realistic task banks is limited.

This paper reports a narrowly framed, preregistered, paired experiment that asks the specific research question frozen in preregistration c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001: Does coupling an LLM generator with a canonical deterministic network verifier materially reduce the proportion of LLM candidates that would execute with operational faults compared to executing the same candidate without verification when the identical candidate is evaluated under both conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics)? Our contribution is an artifact‑grounded report that (1) provides exact deterministic execution counts and inferential outputs for a completed run of 72 paired intents; (2) interprets a degenerate confirmatory outcome (zero baseline faults) and explains its methodological implications; and (3) outlines experimentally grounded recommendations to measure verifier utility under non‑degenerate error regimes.
sections.related_work:
Intent→configuration translation with LLMs has been demonstrated in constrained settings and dialect subsets with measurable task accuracy [1]. Tool‑augmented and multi‑agent frameworks propose integrating validators and orchestrators to reduce regressions in NetOps workflows; system prototypes illustrate possible integrations but typically lack standardized, preregistered end‑to‑end evaluation of verifier detection performance on execution outcomes [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures are proposed and empirically instantiated in code repair and regulated engineering domains to combine stochastic generation with deterministic checks [3]; adapting such architectures to network protocol semantics is a natural but underexplored path. Classical network verification techniques (e.g., header‑space analysis) provide efficient reachability and policy checks and are natural verifier candidates for GVR stacks in NetOps [4].

Our study contributes a preregistered, deterministic test that couples an LLM generator (declared model gpt-5-mini) with a canonical deterministic network verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and reports exact emulator outcomes and validator traces. Where prior work documents architectural proposals or constrained demonstrations, this paper supplies precise paired inference under shared_initial_candidate semantics and deterministic accounting to make clear what this design can and cannot reveal about verifier utility.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) and froze hypotheses, sampling, and analysis code before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory hypothesis H1 prespecified a two‑sided paired binary test (McNemar‑style exact) with target detectable absolute paired reduction 0.20, alpha = 0.05, power >= 0.80, and sample size N = 72 paired intents stratified across three topology complexity strata.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and design consequences. Per the preregistered execution_contract the adapter produced one identical initial generation per intent (one model call) and that same candidate was evaluated in both baseline (execute) and guarded (verify‑then‑execute‑if‑not‑flagged) conditions. Under guarded, verifier flags render the outcome "prevented" (no execution); if the verifier does not flag, the identical candidate is executed. This design isolates verifier detection performance on identical outputs and intentionally avoids conflating generator‑variation effects. By construction, the design cannot capture benefits that arise only through allowed repair calls or through generating alternative candidates in the guarded arm.

Model, adapter, and verifier. The recorded model configuration declares requested_model = "gpt-5-mini" (execution/model_configuration.json). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version recorded as "5.0" in validator traces). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 72, completed_episode_count = 144 (72 pairs × 2 conditions), and failed_episode_count = 0. The model_configuration artifact shows sampling fields unset (temperature = null); that value indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is archived in execution/model_configuration.json (this residual sampling‑parameter uncertainty is explicitly acknowledged in Methods and Threats to Validity).

Task bank, constraints, and contamination controls. Tasks were generated by a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest entry contains the intent, required_command sequence, allowed_touched_fields, expected_final_state, and difficulty metadata (level, pattern, required_command_count). Exact‑match contamination checks against public corpora were applied per the preregistration; confirmatory analysis excluded exact matches. In the executed run no confirmatory pairs were excluded (contamination_summary.csv is empty). Representative manifest entries and their constraints are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

Execution, retries, and scoring. The preregistered missingness_plan permitted up to two additional retries for transient provider errors; the run used no transient retries because provider_call_audit shows completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = hosted_model_call_event_count = 72 and failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0. Validator scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with rule full_intent_constraint_validation; each episode records a binary score and a detailed validator_trace containing parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before and validation_after states, normalized_configuration, and score_reason_code. Scoring artifacts are archived under execution/scoring/*.json.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic consistency. The preregistered run completed without technical failures. Key deterministic counts from archived artifacts are: planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72; complete_pair_count = 72. Provider_call_audit and deterministic_reconciliation.json confirm that all planned stages executed and that cross‑condition cache reuse was not observed (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 72; cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false).

Primary contingency and inferential outputs. The paired contingency table aggregated across 72 pairs is: n_11 = 72 (baseline succeeded and guarded succeeded), n_10 = 0 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n_01 = 0 (guarded failed, baseline succeeded), n_00 = 0 (both failed). The estimated paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline success_rate = 1.0 and guarded success_rate = 1.0. These numeric artifacts are archived and hashed in analysis/*.csv so every reported principal number is verifiable in the evidence bundle.

Representative validator traces and difficulty strata. Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json through task-000006-*.json) show that the verifier parsed and validated each shared candidate: validator_trace fields include parsed_command_count (2–6 depending on task difficulty), required_command_count, difficulty.level (medium/hard/very_hard), normalized_configuration, validation_before and validation_after states, validator_id = "deterministic_netops_validator_v5", validator_version = "5.0", and score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION" for these examples. The stored difficulty strata metadata support descriptive stratified inspection (task counts per difficulty level and per‑stratum summaries are present in analysis artifacts). For this confirmatory sample every shared candidate was accepted by the verifier and produced no emulator‑observed fault in execution.

Interpretation of a degenerate confirmatory outcome. The inferential outputs are degenerate because there was no variation across pairs: the bootstrap CI collapsed to a point and the exact test reports no evidence of a difference (p = 1.0). This outcome is internally consistent and precisely reflects the preregistered estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics: a verifier cannot reduce undetected executed faults if none were observed in baseline executions of the identical candidates.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory interpretation and ceiling effect. The preregistered paired design validly measures whether a verifier detects faults in identical generator outputs. Observing zero baseline faults yields a scientifically informative null/ceiling outcome: for the chosen model, prompt/template, and task bank the generator outputs were uniformly valid on the emulated tasks, and the verifier produced no additional prevention. This does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in general; rather it highlights that verifier utility is conditional on generator error prevalence and on evaluation design choices.

Design implications and recommended follow‑on experiments. The archived artifacts indicate three experimentally grounded modifications to reveal verifier benefit in future studies: (1) permit independent per‑condition generation or multiple stochastic generations per task to increase generator variability and raise baseline error prevalence; (2) incorporate an explicit repair arm (allowed repair calls per preregistration) whose outcomes are recorded to measure repair‑mediated improvements; and (3) assemble adversarial/fault‑injection task sets that intentionally stress semantic ordering and protocol constraints so that baseline failure rates are nontrivial. All three options are compatible with the GVR architecture and are necessary to evaluate false‑positive/false‑negative tradeoffs and operator workload implications.

Threats to validity and operational interpretation. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate semantics deliberately isolates verifier detection on identical outputs but prevents measurement of benefits emerging from additional guarded‑arm generation or repair. Construct validity: our outcome (emulator‑observed faults) is a conservative proxy for operational harm but cannot capture traffic‑dependent, temporal, or large‑scale production effects absent from emulation. External validity: experiments used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic/emulated topologies; results do not generalize across models, vendor dialects, or live devices. Conclusion validity: with zero baseline failures the stated power target (detecting a 0.20 paired reduction) could not be realized—the design produced a ceiling null. These validity considerations are supported by deterministic_reconciliation.json and analysis artifacts and should guide interpretation.

Reproducibility and artifact grounding. All raw and derived artifacts are archived and hashed in the evidence bundle. Key reproducibility anchors include: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and deterministic_reconciliation.json. The bootstrap parameters (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and analysis executor identity (paired_binary_analysis_v1) are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Reproduction consists of loading the archived inputs and running the deterministic analysis executor with the provided input_results_sha256; the stored artifacts are the authoritative trace of execution and analysis.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics (72 confirmatory pairs) to measure whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator‑observed faults; consequently the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). This evidence‑grounded result is conditional: verifier benefit depends on generator error prevalence and task realism. Measuring verifier utility under realistic error regimes requires designs that (a) allow independent or multiple stochastic generations per condition, (b) include adversarial/fault‑injection tasks, and (c) compare across multiple models and sampling settings. We release deterministic execution manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support replication and follow‑on studies.

disclosure_statement: Autonomy and artifacts: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock. Human role: a Research Director selected the topic family and approved the immutable initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; no human manually edited technical manuscript content after the lock. Models and tools: initial generation used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json) orchestrated via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as the canonical verifier; an isolated emulator executed candidate configurations. Preregistration: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 was preregistered and frozen before observing outcomes. Immutable master prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution artifacts and deterministic analysis logs (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json, execution/model_configuration.json, and others) are archived in the registered evidence bundle and contain the authoritative recorded model configuration (including temperature = null), provider call audit counts, and validator traces. No human manual manuscript editing or content insertion occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit under the executed design.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is a recorded residual uncertainty.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
